newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's economic plan turns three amid warnings.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's economic plan turns three amid warnings.

text.p: Brazil celebrated the third anniversary of an inflation-busting economic plan on Tuesday amid warnings that more must be done to avoid a return of multi-digit prices and financial chaos.

Politicians, businessmen and economists across the country toasted the success of the Real Plan, which has slashed inflation from about 5,000 percent in 1994 to about 10 percent last year, its lowest level since 1957.
But all agreed the government has to win its toughest battle yet and implement deep, structural reforms if the plan is not to go the way of failed economic "miracles" of the past.

"Just when we're about to really take off, I find it hard to believe that we're being held back by senseless arguments and by cowardice," President Fernando Henrique Cardoso told a gathering of the country's top businessmen in Brasilia.

He called on Brazil's Congress to vote quickly on reforms of an overstaffed civil service and an endebted pensions system, both of which are considered crucial to Cardoso's plan to turn Brazil into an economic powerhouse.

The bills were sent to parliament two years ago but have run into stiff opposition among lawmakers fearful of losing votes in next year's elections and many of whose backers stand to lose out from the changes.

Cardoso said he wanted to see real progress over the reforms in an extraordinary sesssion of Congress called to run through the July recess in an attempt to make up for lost time. "The time has come: either certain reforms are voted now or we have no resources to make further progress," he said.

Many observers believe Cardoso's reform push has already failed, for now. With next year's elections looming large, and his own re-election campaign to worry about, the bills may have to wait until the next Congress sits in 1999, they say.

The propsect of that kind of delay did not find much support among the businessmen listening to Cardoso's speech. "The economic reforms cannot wait until 1999 because that would be a fatal blow against Brazilian economic growth," Jorge Gerdau, the owner of one of Brazil's biggest steel companies, said.

A recent study by Sao Paulo's Industry Federation suggested Brazil's pace of economic growth would double to about 7 percent if the reforms were approved, finally putting the country on course to meet its long-awaited potential.

"Brazil can either double the size of its entire economy in 10 years or it can carry on at the same pace and take 23 years to do the same," said Gerdau, who represents Brazil's National Industry Confederation.
